parsed.canonical_question: How do NADH and FADH2 feed electrons into the transport chain?

rendering.title: NADH and FADH2 as electron donors
rendering.explanation:
NADH and FADH2 are electron carrier molecules produced during glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. They deliver high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain, which is a series of protein complexes embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

NADH donates its electrons at Complex I (also called NADH dehydrogenase). When NADH binds to Complex I, it is oxidised back to NAD+, releasing two electrons. Complex I passes those electrons along and uses the released energy to pump four protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space.

FADH2 donates its electrons at Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase). FADH2 is oxidised back to FAD, releasing two electrons. Complex II passes these electrons into the chain as well, but it does not directly pump any protons across the membrane. Because FADH2 enters the chain at a lower energy point than NADH, each FADH2 ultimately results in fewer protons pumped and therefore less ATP produced.

From Complexes I and II, electrons are passed to a mobile carrier called ubiquinone (coenzyme Q), which carries them to Complex III. From Complex III, another mobile carrier, cytochrome c, shuttles electrons to Complex IV, where they are finally passed to oxygen to form water.

The protons pumped by Complexes I, III, and IV build up the proton gradient that drives ATP synthase. This is why NADH and FADH2 are so important: they are the link between the chemical energy in glucose and the proton gradient that powers most of the cell's ATP production.
summary_bullets: NADH donates electrons at Complex I, which pumps four protons per NADH oxidised.
FADH2 donates electrons at Complex II, which does not directly pump protons, giving FADH2 a lower ATP yield.
Electrons pass from both entry points through ubiquinone to Complex III, then via cytochrome c to Complex IV.
The proton gradient built up by the chain drives ATP synthase to make ATP.
